newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: CZECH FINMIN BACKS TAX SURCHARGE TO AID BUDGET - CTK.
newsitem.headline: CZECH FINMIN BACKS TAX SURCHARGE TO AID BUDGET - CTK.

text.p: Czech Finance Minister Ivan Pilip said on Monday that recent floods would make it practically impossible to balance the 1997 budget and he would propose a tax surcharge for extra revenue, the CTK news agency reported.

It quoted Pilip before a meeting of the leadership of his Civic Democratic Party (ODS) as saying he would recommend a limited-time surcharge on some existing taxes to finance relief efforts after massive July floods in the east of the country.

"For technical reasons I would not recommend a fully special tax, but from a technical point of view there can be a special and time-limited surcharge toward some of the existing types of taxes," it quoted Pilip as saying.

The 1997 budget, originally approved as balanced, showed a seven-month deficit of 8.8 billion crowns after a slowdown in economic growth in the first half of the year made revenues fall short of expectations.
CTK quoted Pilip in indirect speech as saying he believed that it would be "practically impossible" for the 1997 budget to end in balance, but the story did not elaborate.
The governing coalition promised a balanced 1997 budget after making 45.5 billion crowns in spending cuts on the heels of speculative attackS on the crown in April in May.
But private economists have forecast the budget would still end with a deficit totalling from seven to 20 billion crowns.
Many economists have called for a surplus budget to help slow domestic demand which fuelled the massive current account deficit which brought on the attacks on the crown.
Several politicians have suggested flood reconstruction funds should come from a special income tax hike -- which the central bank has supported -- or a hike in the value added tax on consumption.

The daily Mlada Fronta Dnes on Saturday quoted unnamed sources as saying the finance ministry was mulling options such as an additional seven percent surcharge on personal and corporate income tax or a half-crown surcharge on petrol.
No concrete proposal for additional taxes has been submitted by the government, but one is widely expected soon.
A government estimate put total flood damage to crops, homes, businesses and infrastructure at 60 billion crowns.
The cabinet has approved five billion crowns in flood relief bonds and roughly eight billion crowns in further spending from on-budget and off-budget revenue sources.
Several more billions of crowns are expected from international organisations either through grants or credits.
